title: The ships that came home with coin
learnerQuestion: Where did Manila's spring ships come home to around 1602, who licensed them, and what did the port do when they came back carrying little but silver coin?
sensitiveContentNotice: Two parts of this Story, "Two ways of telling it" and "October 1603, from home", tell of the killing of many Chinese residents of Manila in 1603. The first also tells of a man beheaded.

paragraphs.text: This view is of 1602, at Haicheng, a port in Fujian on the south-east coast of China. Its older name was Yuegang, the Moon Harbour.
Ships licensed here sailed in the spring for Luzon, the island where the Spaniards held Manila.
No one we have read describes the port in 1602 itself. The witnesses stand some years to either side.

About 1608 an English merchant at Bantam, in Java, wrote down what was known there of the Chinese ships that sailed to Manila. Nothing we have read puts him in China. Out they carried, he wrote, 'raw and wrought Silkes': silk, raw and worked.
'In the beginning of Iune [June] they returne', he went on. 'Their lading [cargo] is Rialls of eight.' Reals of eight were Spanish silver coins.

By 1589 the customs officers at Haicheng had said the same, as the historian Richard von Glahn reports it: ships from Luzon came home with no cargo except silver coins. Duty was charged on goods, and coin was not goods.
How a harbour the law had forbidden came to license these ships, what it did about the coin, and what the trade cost the people who sailed, is the Story.
Before 1567 the court of the Ming dynasty, which ruled China, forbade its people to go abroad to trade. Yuegang, in the Zhangzhou estuary, traded anyway.
The coast had been raided for years. The raiders are called 'Japanese pirates'. The historian Pin-tsun Chang writes that they were mainly Chinese and Japanese armed smugglers.

Some officials came to think that trade, not force, would end the raiding. One of them, Tang Shu, wrote in the 1550s, in Chang's translation: 'if trade is open to them, pirates will turn into traders; if closed, they will turn into pirates.'
In 1567 a new emperor, Longqing, came to the throne. The governor of Fujian, Tu Zemin, sent the court a memorial, a written proposal, asking it to open the trade. The court agreed.
The memorial itself is not in the court's own record. We know of it because a later governor, Xu Fuyuan, mentioned it in 1594.
The court made Yuegang a county seat and named it Haicheng. The county lay in Zhangzhou prefecture, in the province of Fujian. The licensed trade was based there.

The opening was narrow. Each ship's captain needed a licence. The court fixed how many there were, and they were issued at Haicheng. A ship could carry out no sulphur, copper or iron, which von Glahn calls strategic materials, and it had to be home within a year. Foreigners still could not come to China to trade freely, and Japan stayed forbidden.
The trade was taxed in two ways: a fee on each ship by its measured size, and duty on the goods.
In 1571, four years after the opening, the Spaniards settled at Manila with silver from America. Manila soon became one of the places the licensed ships went.
Haicheng's merchants pressed the Ming authorities for more licences to go there. In 1589 the court fixed the number of licences at 88. Sixteen were for Luzon, more than for any other place.
By 1597 Haicheng was issuing 137. How many of those were for Manila is not known.

The ships came home with coin and little else. So in 1589, von Glahn writes, the customs put a flat charge of 150 taels on every ship back from Luzon. A tael was a Chinese unit of weight used to reckon silver. The next year the charge was 120. No Source we have read says why it fell.

The silver the port took in fees and duties grew: some 3,000 taels a year in its first years, more than 20,000 in 1583, more than 29,000 in 1594. About 1599 it was more than 27,000. No figure for 1602 is in the Sources we have read.
Historians read the rise as the port's trade growing and foreign silver coming in. That silver came from Japan as well as from Manila, and the figures do not say how much came from each.

The historian James Chin writes that most of the Chinese who lived at Manila came from Zhangzhou prefecture, and notably from Haicheng and two other counties. A Fujian historian of the time, He Qiaoyuan (1557–1631), wrote that because Luzon was so near, most Zhangzhou people who travelled went there. We have his words in Chin's translation.
Some came over each year with the ships. Others stayed at Manila as their agents, sold the goods for silver, and gathered a cargo for the voyage home.

A later official, Fu Yuanchu, put the trade in a sentence in 1639, here in Chang's translation: those who go to Luzon 'will simply exchange for silver coins'. He believed Luzon had a silver mountain. In fact the silver at Manila was American, shipped across the Pacific from Acapulco.

The merchants of this coast took their gods with them. Chin writes that the goddess Mazu and other gods of southern Fujian were carried to Chinese settlements overseas, where temples became meeting places.
The examples he gives are other ports, not Manila.

At Manila, Dominican missionaries built a church near the Chinese quarter soon after they arrived in 1587. Before that, Chinese who became Christians had been expected to cut their long hair and dress as Spaniards. The historian John Wills writes that it is not clear how far the Dominicans changed this.
No Source we have read names a temple, a god or a rite at Haicheng itself.
In the early 1590s Japan invaded Korea. Some officials wanted the sea closed again, to cut off contact with the Japanese, and the court shut the trade.
Officials in Fujian protested. Xu Fuyuan, the governor who mentioned Tu Zemin's memorial, was among them. By 1594 the trade was open, with Japan still forbidden.
Not every ship had stopped. In 1592, during the ban, more than twenty Chinese ships reached Manila.

Nor did every ship keep to its licence. Spanish records show more Chinese ships at Manila than the licences allowed. An official with the title of censor wrote in 1623 that ships licensed for other ports had gone to Manila.

From 1596 the next emperor, Wanli, sent eunuchs into the provinces to collect taxes and run mines. Eunuchs were men of the palace staff. The emperor sent them himself, and they took over work that the regular civil officials had done.
Historians call these men commissioners. By 1599 the main ports each had one. In Fujian, historians name him as Gao Cai, and one adds that the duties on the sea trade were part of his charge.

In 1602, the year of this view, the commissioner in Fujian obtained the emperor's leave to look for precious metals on a mountain across the sea. A man from Fujian named Zhang Yi had told of it; Wills calls him an adventurer. Officials at court protested.

The mountain was said to be at Cavite, beside Manila. The historian Ray Huang writes that there is no evidence the emperor knew where it was. No Source we have read joins this mountain to the silver mountain Fu Yuanchu wrote of a generation later.
In 1603 officials from Fujian sailed to Manila to see the mountain. One of them was Wang Shihe, an official of Haicheng county.

That October, at Manila, very many of the Chinese who lived there were killed, by Spanish soldiers and by the Japanese soldiers and the men of Pampanga and the Tagalog provinces who fought beside them.

Historians give different totals. Borao writes that some 20,000 Chinese were killed. Wills writes of more than twenty thousand, and says estimates range from fifteen thousand to twenty-five thousand. Borao reports that the Ming Shi, a Chinese history, says twenty-five thousand. We have read no count made at the time.
The voyage, the commissioner's part in it, and the blame afterwards are told in more than one way.
Both columns below are the words of officials and churchmen. No account by any of the Chinese residents who were killed is presented here.

beats.sensitiveNotice: This part tells of the killing of Chinese residents of Manila in 1603, of who was blamed for it, and of a man beheaded. It gives historians' estimates of the number killed.

note.text: Provincial officials and the court's own historians, as later historians report them. They had opposed the search for gold and were at odds with the commissioner. After the killing at Manila they had reason to show that the blame lay elsewhere.

Officials and churchmen of a small colony: some 700 Spaniards and Mexicans in a city with many thousand Chinese. In 1593 conscripted Chinese rowers had killed a governor. The governor's own account was written to the king after the killing, to explain his conduct, and the day-by-day reports come from two judges who were hostile to him. No historian we have read names a motive beyond these.

cells.text: The officer who wrote ahead to Manila said he did not believe in the mountain, and that it was his duty to look.
Wills writes that the province sent the party to show up Zhang Yi's story.
The Spaniards could not believe that was the purpose. Rumour spread that the visitors had come to spy for an invasion.

segments.text: Borao writes that the Chinese and Spanish sources agree on one point: this voyage caused the Spaniards' suspicion.

cells.text: To 'the scholars and civil officials', Wills writes, the affair was a case of 'collusion between eunuchs and seagoing Chinese desperadoes'. The court record, in Borao's translation, says Zhang Yi meant 'to conspire with the eunuchs'.

These are not a Spaniard's own views. A Dominican at Manila, Benavides, wrote down what the Chinese there were saying: that the eunuchs laid many taxes on the people to get gold and silver for the emperor, and that within two years or so there would be risings in China.

segments.text: Wills notes that the Chinese record of these years is rich because officials were fighting the palace commissioners. Huang adds that the regular officials had run the same taxes laxly and corruptly themselves. Borao finds that the sources do not agree on what Gao Cai's part was.

cells.text: The officials of Fujian laid much of the blame on Zhang Yi. The court record says he was beheaded.
Governor Acuña told the king it had been stirred up from China.

segments.text: A Chinese history written about 1653 says the officials of Fujian and Guangdong 'only told the emperor half the truth'. We have it in Borao's translation.

provenanceLine.text: Gao Cai left no account that we have read. The Chinese records reach us through historians who translate or summarise them: José Eugenio Borao, John Wills and Ray Huang. The Spanish side is told more fully in the Story "The spring ships".

closingParagraphs.text: Historians do not agree on who sailed. Borao, working from Spanish reports, has three officials landing on 23 May. The letter they carried named a eunuch, and Borao reasons that the third official was Gao Cai himself.
Wills has two officials, arriving in March, with Zhang Yi in chains, and no commissioner. Borao writes that Wang Shihe was so distraught over the expedition that he died soon after he reached Fujian.

paragraphs.text: The killing of October 1603 is told in the Story "The spring ships", in its part "The massacre of 1603", with the Spanish and Chinese accounts side by side.
Most of Manila's Chinese had come from this coast, and Haicheng is one of the counties named.
The officials of Fujian told Manila to send the widows and orphans of the dead home. China sent no fleet to punish the killing.
No Source we have read says how the news reached Haicheng, or what was said there.

Of such merchants in general, Chin says, drawing on Fujian writers of about 1630: a man abroad might be gone for many years, and some came home to grown sons they did not know. Nothing we have read ties these accounts to the families of 1603.
The trade did not stop. Ships from China were at Manila again in 1604.
That year the governor of Fujian, Xu Xueju, wrote that his people traded at Luzon only for the silver coins to be had there.

The commissioner appears once more. In 1604 a Dutch squadron came to the Penghu Islands, shown on the map off this coast, to ask for trade. Men from Haicheng who traded at Patani, on the Malay Peninsula, had advised the Dutch. One of them, Li Jin, told them to pay the commissioner. Gao Cai sent word, Wills writes, that leave to trade could be had for forty to fifty thousand reals.
A naval officer, Shen Yourong, came with fifty war junks and told the Dutch to leave. They found no harbour that suited them and gave up. No Source we have read says they paid.

beats.sensitiveNotice: This part tells of the killing of Chinese residents of Manila in 1603, as it bore on the coast they came from. It gives no count.

paragraphs.text: Much of what historians say about this port goes back to one local book, Zhang Xie's study of the Eastern and Western Oceans, written in 1616 and printed at Zhangzhou the next year. We have not read it.
By the middle of the 1600s Haicheng's sea trade was over. Most of its merchants, it seems, had moved to Xiamen, another port in southern Fujian.

**Not yet researched.** This Story stops in 1604. Where the coin went after the quay, who the merchants of 1602 were, and how the port's trade ended have not been researched, so none is offered as a researched path. When a path is researched, it will appear here with its own Claims and Evidence.
